text: Chest tightness: Shortness of breath (SOB), known as dyspnea or dyspnoea, is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough. The American Thoracic Society defines it as "a subjective experience of breathing discomfort that consists of qualitatively distinct sensations that vary in intensity", and recommends evaluating dyspnea by assessing the intensity of its distinct sensations, the degree of distress and discomfort involved, and its burden or impact on the patient's activities of daily living.

Cough: A cough is a sudden expulsion of air through the large breathing passages which can help clear them of fluids, irritants, foreign particles and microbes. As a protective reflex, coughing can be repetitive with the cough reflex following three phases: an inhalation, a forced exhalation against a closed glottis, and a violent release of air from the lungs following opening of the glottis, usually accompanied by a distinctive sound.
Fever with cough: A presenting complaint characterised by fever with cough.

Hemoptysis: Hemoptysis or haemoptysis is the discharge of blood or blood-stained mucus through the mouth coming from the bronchi, larynx, trachea, or lungs. In other words, it is the airway bleeding, and does not necessarily involve coughing.
Night sweats: Night sweats or nocturnal hyperhydrosis is the repeated occurrence of excessive sweating during sleep. The person may or may not also perspire excessively while awake.

Pleuritic chest pain: Pleurisy, also known as pleuritis, is inflammation of the membranes that surround the lungs and line the chest cavity (pleurae). This can result in a sharp chest pain while breathing.

Productive cough: A cough is a sudden expulsion of air through the large breathing passages which can help clear them of fluids, irritants, foreign particles and microbes. As a protective reflex, coughing can be repetitive with the cough reflex following three phases: an inhalation, a forced exhalation against a closed glottis, and a violent release of air from the lungs following opening of the glottis, usually accompanied by a distinctive sound.

Shortness of breath: Shortness of breath (SOB), known as dyspnea or dyspnoea, is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough. The American Thoracic Society defines it as "a subjective experience of breathing discomfort that consists of qualitatively distinct sensations that vary in intensity", and recommends evaluating dyspnea by assessing the intensity of its distinct sensations, the degree of distress and discomfort involved, and its burden or impact on the patient's activities of daily living.

Stridor: Stridor is an extra-thoracic high-pitched breath sound resulting from turbulent air flow in the larynx or elsewhere in the upper respiratory tract. It is different from stertor, which is a snoring noise originating in the pharynx, and wheezing, which originates in the bronchi.

Wheezing: A wheeze is a clinical symptom of a continuous, coarse, whistling sound produced in the respiratory airways during breathing. For wheezes to occur, part of the respiratory tree must be narrowed or obstructed, or airflow velocity within the respiratory tree must be heightened.

Acute Bronchitis: A respiratory condition known as Acute Bronchitis. Common presenting complaints: Cough, Productive Cough, Chest Tightness, Fever With Cough. Associated symptoms: Wheeze, Low Grade Fever, Malaise. Risk factors: Recent Viral Infection, Smoking, Cold Weather. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.

Acute Bronchitis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Asthma: Asthma features recurrent discrete episodes triggered by allergens/exercise with reversible airflow obstruction; acute bronchitis is entirely self-limiting with no episodic wheeze. Compared to Pneumonia: Pneumonia features focal consolidation on CXR, high fever >38.5°C, and productive purulent sputum; acute bronchitis shows a clear CXR and milder systemic symptoms.

Asthma: Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways. It is characterized by variable and recurring symptoms and reduced lung function. Common presenting complaints: Wheezing, Shortness Of Breath, Chest Tightness, Cough. Associated symptoms: Expiratory Wheeze, Nocturnal Symptoms, Exercise Induced Bronchospasm, Reversible Airflow Obstruction. Risk factors: Atopy, Family History Asthma, Air Pollution Exposure, Smoking, Occupational Allergens. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Asthma red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_004) triggered by complaint 'SHORTNESS_OF_BREATH': Acute severe asthma — no improvement after reliever use. Red flag (RED_RESP_001) triggered by complaint 'SHORTNESS_OF_BREATH': Sudden severe breathlessness in known asthmatic.

Asthma differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Copd: COPD is associated with a history of heavy smoking and shows fixed airflow obstruction (post-BD FEV1/FVC <0.7); asthma shows reversible obstruction and onset is typically younger with atopic history. Compared to Acute Bronchitis: Acute bronchitis is self-limiting with no episodic wheeze; asthma features recurrent discrete episodes triggered by allergens/exercise with reversible airflow obstruction.

Bronchiectasis: Bronchiectasis is a disease in which there is permanent enlargement of parts of the airways of the lung. Symptoms typically include a chronic cough with mucus production. Common presenting complaints: Productive Cough, Hemoptysis, Cough. Associated symptoms: Recurrent Respiratory Infections, Copious Sputum, Finger Clubbing. Risk factors: Recurrent Respiratory Infections, Cystic Fibrosis, Immunodeficiency, Chronic Aspiration. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Bronchiectasis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Copd: COPD has diffuse airflow obstruction without bronchial dilatation; bronchiectasis shows dilated bronchi on HRCT with copious daily sputum production and recurrent infections.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term lung condition that makes it progressively harder to breathe. It occurs when the airways and lung tissue become damaged, leading to reduced airflow and reduced efficiency of oxygen exchange in the lungs. Common presenting complaints: Shortness Of Breath, Productive Cough, Cough, Chest Tightness, Wheezing. Associated symptoms: Chronic Productive Cough, Exercise Intolerance, Barrel Chest, Pursed Lip Breathing. Risk factors: Smoking, Biomass Fuel Exposure, Older Age, Air Pollution Exposure, Alpha1 Antitrypsin Deficiency. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_005) triggered by complaint 'SHORTNESS_OF_BREATH': Respiratory failure — oxygen saturation critically low. Red flag (RED_RESP_001) triggered by complaint 'SHORTNESS_OF_BREATH': Sudden severe breathlessness in COPD patient.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Asthma: Asthma shows fully reversible obstruction and often has atopy; COPD shows fixed post-BD obstruction predominantly in older smokers. Compared to Interstitial Lung Disease: ILD shows restrictive spirometry (reduced TLC) with fine bibasal crackles; COPD shows obstructive spirometry and hyperinflation with coarse breath sounds. Compared to Bronchiectasis: Bronchiectasis shows dilated bronchi on HRCT with copious daily sputum production and recurrent infections; COPD has diffuse airflow obstruction without bronchial dilatation.

Interstitial Lung Disease: A respiratory condition known as Interstitial Lung Disease. Common presenting complaints: Shortness Of Breath, Cough, Chest Tightness. Associated symptoms: Finger Clubbing, Fine Crackles Bibasal, Exercise Intolerance. Risk factors: Occupational Dust Exposure, Connective Tissue Disease, Drug Toxicity, Older Age. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Interstitial Lung Disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Copd: COPD is obstructive with hyperinflation; ILD is restrictive with reduced DLCO and fine bibasal crackles — spirometry pattern is key distinguishing feature.

Lung Cancer: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor that originates in the tissues of the lungs. Lung cancer is caused by genetic damage to the DNA of cells in the airways, often caused by cigarette smoking or inhaling damaging chemicals. Common presenting complaints: Cough, Hemoptysis, Shortness Of Breath, Chest Tightness. Associated symptoms: Weight Loss, Fatigue, Hoarseness, Finger Clubbing. Risk factors: Smoking, Radon Exposure, Asbestos Exposure, Family History Lung Cancer, Older Age. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Lung Cancer red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_002) triggered by complaint 'HEMOPTYSIS': Haemoptysis with night sweats — suspected malignancy.

Lung Cancer differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pulmonary Tuberculosis: TB is associated with contact history, AFB-positive sputum, and upper lobe infiltrates; lung cancer is associated with smoking/age, hemoptysis, and a discrete mass on CT. Compared to Pleural Effusion: Pleural effusion can be a complication of lung cancer (malignant effusion) but also occurs in heart failure, infection, and liver disease — cytology and LDH/protein ratio differentiate.

Pleural Effusion: A respiratory condition known as Pleural Effusion. Common presenting complaints: Shortness Of Breath, Pleuritic Chest Pain, Cough. Associated symptoms: Reduced Breath Sounds, Dullness To Percussion. Risk factors: Heart Failure, Malignancy, Pneumonia, Liver Disease. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.

Pleural Effusion differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Lung Cancer: Cytology and LDH/protein ratio distinguish generic effusion from lung cancer; effusion can be a complication of lung cancer (malignant effusion) but also occurs in heart failure/infection. Compared to Pneumothorax: Pneumothorax shows absent breath sounds with hyper-resonance on percussion; pleural effusion shows absent breath sounds with dullness to percussion.

Pneumonia: Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition of the lung primarily affecting the small air sacs known as alveoli. Symptoms typically include some combination of productive or dry cough, chest pain, fever, and difficulty breathing. Common presenting complaints: Fever With Cough, Productive Cough, Shortness Of Breath, Pleuritic Chest Pain. Associated symptoms: Fever, Rigors, Malaise, Bronchial Breath Sounds. Risk factors: Older Age, Immunocompromised, Smoking, Chronic Lung Disease, Recent Viral Infection. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.
Pneumonia red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_005) triggered by complaint 'FEVER_WITH_COUGH': Respiratory failure in severe pneumonia.

Pneumonia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pulmonary Tuberculosis: TB has gradual onset with >3 weeks of cough, night sweats, and upper lobe CXR changes; community pneumonia has acute onset with lobar consolidation and responds to standard antibiotics. Compared to Acute Bronchitis: Acute bronchitis shows a clear CXR and milder systemic symptoms; pneumonia features focal consolidation on CXR, high fever >38.5°C, and productive purulent sputum.

Pneumothorax: A pneumothorax is collection of air in the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall. Symptoms typically include sudden onset of sharp, one-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. Common presenting complaints: Shortness Of Breath, Pleuritic Chest Pain, Chest Tightness. Associated symptoms: Tachycardia, Reduced Breath Sounds Unilateral. Risk factors: Tall Thin Habitus, Smoking, Connective Tissue Disorder, Trauma. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: male_predominant. Acute or chronic: acute.

Pneumothorax red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_003) triggered by complaint 'SHORTNESS_OF_BREATH': Tension pneumothorax — sudden breathlessness with tracheal deviation. Red flag (RED_RESP_001) triggered by complaint 'PLEURITIC_CHEST_PAIN': Sudden severe breathlessness with pleuritic pain — suspected pneumothorax.

Pneumothorax differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pleural Effusion: Pleural effusion causes dullness to percussion; pneumothorax causes hyper-resonance — both reduce breath sounds but are distinguished by percussion note and CXR.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A respiratory condition known as Pulmonary Tuberculosis. Common presenting complaints: Cough, Hemoptysis, Night Sweats, Fever With Cough. Associated symptoms: Weight Loss, Fatigue, Afternoon Fever, Anorexia. Risk factors: Hiv Infection, Close Tb Contact, Malnutrition, Overcrowding, Diabetes. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis red flags. Red flag (RED_RESP_002) triggered by complaint 'HEMOPTYSIS': Haemoptysis with night sweats — suspected TB. Red flag (RED_RESP_006) triggered by complaint 'FEVER_WITH_COUGH': Suspected active pulmonary TB with close contacts.

Pulmonary Tuberculosis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pneumonia: Community pneumonia has acute onset with lobar consolidation and responds to standard antibiotics; TB has gradual onset with >3 weeks of cough, night sweats, and upper lobe CXR changes. Compared to Lung Cancer: Lung cancer rarely causes fever and responds poorly to antibiotics; TB features systemic symptoms (night sweats, weight loss) and AFB positivity on sputum microscopy.
Sudden severe breathlessness - action: emergency pathway.
Haemoptysis with night sweats — suspected malignancy or TB - action: urgent respiratory evaluation.
Tension pneumothorax signs - action: emergency pathway.
Acute severe asthma — no response to bronchodilator - action: emergency pathway.
Respiratory failure — oxygen saturation < 92% - action: emergency pathway.
Suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis with close contacts - action: tb isolation pathway.
